strengths: The paper asks a timely and well-defined mechanistic question: whether verbal confidence is computed just-in-time at the confidence prompt or cached earlier near answer generation, and whether it is reducible to token likelihoods.

The evidence is unusually convergent for this kind of claim: activation steering, patching, noising, swapping, probing, and attention blocking all point to PANL and CC as behaviorally relevant positions, with a consistent earlier-to-later layer pattern from PANL to CC.
The authors include meaningful controls, including PANL+1/FCC positions, same-confidence swap controls, categorical and numeric confidence prompts, and a second architecture (Qwen 2.5 7B).
The manuscript is generally clear and the appendix provides useful methodological detail, including sample sizes, layer sweeps, calibration metrics, and definitions of intervention metrics.
weaknesses: The strongest interpretation is overclaimed. The experiments support that confidence-related information is represented at post-answer positions under these prompts, but they do not fully establish an automatic, general-purpose metacognitive computation. PANL occurs after the model has seen the answer and prompt framing, and the generated-answer phase appears not to be exactly identical to the later confidence-rating prefix, weakening the claim that the PANL representation is exactly what would arise during ordinary answer generation.

The claim that verbal confidence is not a token-logprob readout relies on a limited baseline: mean length-normalized answer log-probability. Stronger first-order/fluency baselines such as minimum token logprob, entropy/margin, answer-token trajectory features, alternative-answer likelihoods, or calibrated combinations of logit features are needed before concluding that the representation reflects a richer second-order evaluation.

Attention-blocking null results do not decisively rule out just-in-time computation. Information may already have propagated through intermediate/template tokens before the blocked layer window, and the categorical prompt results explicitly show redundant routing. Thus the evidence against all forms of JIT computation is weaker than the paper’s language suggests.

The empirical scope is narrow: mainly TriviaQA factual short-answer questions, greedy decoding, no chain-of-thought, and mostly Gemma 3 27B, with Qwen results summarized more coarsely. It is unclear whether the mechanism applies to reasoning tasks, open-ended answers, calibrated deployment settings, or models with different instruction tuning.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone: code, seeds, exact dataset splits, generated answers, GPT-4o-mini grading protocol/validation, and details needed to reproduce all interventions are not clearly provided. The reliance on GPT-4o-mini as correctness judge also deserves a stronger validation or sensitivity analysis.

Some controls remain imperfect. PANL+1 and FCC differ substantially in syntax and role from PANL/CC, high/low steering vectors are built from only extreme examples, and several key interventions have small selected samples, which may inflate apparent localization or effect sizes.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and interesting question: whether verbal confidence in LLMs is computed only when requested or whether confidence-relevant information is cached during answer generation and later retrieved.

The experimental toolkit is reasonably broad for a mechanistic-interpretability paper, combining activation steering, patching, noising, activation swaps, linear probes, variance partitioning, and attention blocking.

The causal-intervention results are internally consistent in one important respect: PANL effects tend to appear at earlier layers than CC effects, and PANL+1/FCC controls are usually much weaker. This provides some evidence that answer-adjacent positions are involved in routing confidence information.
The paper makes some effort to test generality beyond the main setup, including a numeric confidence prompt and Qwen 2.5 7B in addition to Gemma 3 27B.
The appendix gives many implementation details, including prompts, layer sweeps, sample sizes for several interventions, definitions of metrics, and calibration plots.
weaknesses: The central interpretation is overclaimed. The evidence shows that confidence-related information can be causally manipulated at PANL and CC, but it does not convincingly establish that the model performs a "sophisticated self-evaluation" or metacognitive computation rather than routing answer/content features that correlate with the later confidence label.

The distinction between cached retrieval and just-in-time computation is not as clean as claimed. The main prompt places confidence instructions after the answer, but the answer generation phase is described as using a related prompt with confidence instructions at the start, and the two-phase construction makes it difficult to interpret claims about what the model computes before it knows confidence will be requested.

The paper’s comparison to token log-probabilities is too weak to support the broad claim that verbal confidence is not a fluency/readout signal. Mean length-normalized answer log-probability is a limited baseline; stronger alternatives such as minimum token probability, answer entropy, margin, sequence likelihood variants, semantic uncertainty, or probes of answer-token hidden states are not adequately ruled out.

The causal interventions have important confounds. Steering vectors are constructed from only 25 high- and 25 low-confidence examples, patching/noising use mean ablation that can introduce distribution shift, and PANL swaps may transfer answer- or prompt-specific information despite length matching. These issues weaken the sufficiency/necessity claims.

The evaluation is narrow: mostly TriviaQA, short factual answers, greedy decoding, and two open-weight instruction models. It is unclear whether the mechanism holds for reasoning tasks, long-form answers, multi-step uncertainty, different calibration regimes, or models whose confidence reports are poorly calibrated.

Some reported effects are partial and modest, yet the prose often treats them as decisive. For example, attention blocking changes around 20% in the minimal prompt and partial recovery/disruption in patching/noising do not fully justify the strong conclusion that the pathway is answer tokens -> PANL -> CC as the operative mechanism.

The paper relies heavily on linear probes and variance partitioning, but probing results are not enough to establish task-relevant computation; although the authors acknowledge this generally, the conclusions still lean too strongly on decodability as evidence of richer answer-quality evaluation.

Reproducibility is incomplete for an ICML main-track mechanistic claim. The manuscript gives many details, but does not clearly provide code, exact data splits, all prompts for phase 0, GPT-4o-mini grading procedures, random seeds, hardware/compute, or enough detail to independently reproduce the full intervention pipeline.

Limitations and ethics are underdeveloped. The paper discusses some methodological caveats locally, but does not sufficiently address risks from automated correctness grading, dataset contamination, prompt dependence, interpretability overclaiming, or downstream misuse of verbal confidence as a reliability signal.

Presentation is readable, but the framing is too assertive. Phrases such as "demonstrate," "rule out," and "sophisticated metacognitive capacity" go beyond what the experiments establish, reducing confidence in the paper’s scientific calibration.

strengths: The paper asks a clear and important mechanistic question: whether verbal confidence is computed just-in-time at the confidence prompt or cached earlier during answer generation, and whether it is reducible to answer token log-probabilities. This is a timely topic for LLM uncertainty and calibration.

The experimental package is unusually convergent. Activation steering, patching, mean ablation/noising, activation swaps, linear probing, variance partitioning, and attention blocking all point toward a consistent cached-retrieval story, with PANL effects emerging earlier than confidence-colon effects.

The causal interventions are more persuasive than a probing-only paper. In particular, the PANL/CC/control-position comparisons, same-confidence versus cross-confidence activation swaps, and attention-blocking experiments provide meaningful evidence that the identified positions participate in the confidence-reporting computation.

The authors include useful robustness checks across categorical and numeric confidence formats, plus a second architecture, Qwen 2.5 7B. The main analysis is centered on Gemma 3 27B, but the additional experiments reduce concern that the result is purely prompt- or model-specific.

The paper is generally well written and well organized. The hypotheses are explicit, the figures support the narrative, and the appendix gives many implementation details such as model versions, layer sweeps, sample sizes, decoding settings, confidence-class tokenization, and intervention definitions.
weaknesses: The central interpretation is somewhat stronger than the evidence warrants. Showing that PANL activations causally affect later verbal confidence supports cached information flow, but the claim that this reflects a sophisticated self-evaluation or metacognitive capacity is not fully established; the representation may still contain task-, answer-, or prompt-specific correlates rather than a general answer-quality evaluation.

The evidence against token log-probability as the relevant first-order signal is suggestive but incomplete. The comparison mainly uses length-normalized answer log-probability, which may be a weak proxy for the richer set of generation-time signals available to the model. Thus, variance beyond this baseline does not by itself prove a genuinely second-order confidence computation.

The scope is narrow: most detailed experiments use TriviaQA and Gemma 3 27B, with limited replication on Qwen and prompt variants. It remains unclear whether the same mechanism holds for reasoning tasks, long-form generation, multi-hop QA, conversational settings, or models whose verbal confidence is poorly calibrated.

Some intervention results are partial and require cautious interpretation. Patching/noising effects do not fully recover or destroy behavior, attention blocking has known limitations because information may have flowed earlier or through redundant paths, and the categorical prompt requires a minimal-prompt variant to reveal the direct CC-to-PANL pathway.

The paper lacks an explicit limitations and ethics section. Given that confidence reports are often used in safety-critical deployment decisions, the manuscript should more directly discuss risks of over-trusting verbal confidence, possible misuse of steering interventions, and the limits of applying these findings to black-box deployed systems.

Reproducibility is decent but not complete. The appendix provides many methodological details, but I did not see a clear code/data release statement, exact dataset split identifiers, full prompt text in extractable form, or enough implementation detail to make the mechanistic interventions easy to reproduce without substantial reimplementation effort.

strengths: The paper studies an important and timely question: how verbal confidence reports are produced internally by LLMs, rather than only whether they are calibrated behaviorally.

The evidence is unusually multi-pronged for a mechanistic interpretability paper: activation steering, patching, noising, swaps, attention blocking, and probing/variance partitioning all point to a special role for the post-answer newline and confidence-colon positions.

The authors include meaningful controls, including adjacent-token controls, answer-colon analyses, same-confidence swap controls, OOD-shift checks, and attention blocking controls. These make the central cached-retrieval story substantially more credible than a single probing result would be.
The paper makes a useful attempt to test generality beyond one setting, including categorical and numeric prompts, Gemma and Qwen, BigMath/MMLU, and a reasoning model with chain-of-thought traces.
Presentation is mostly clear, with helpful experiment roadmaps and detailed appendix methods. The limitations and impact statement are generally appropriate and do not hide the bounded scope.
weaknesses: The central interpretation is stronger than the evidence warrants. PANL and CC clearly carry causal information relevant to confidence output, but the experiments do not fully establish that this is a dedicated confidence representation rather than a mixture of answer identity, correctness, difficulty, plausibility, and prompt-specific evaluative features correlated with confidence.

The claim that verbal confidence is not reducible to token log-probabilities is only tested against a limited set of answer-token log-probability summaries with linear baselines. This does not rule out richer first-order generation signals, full logit distributions, entropy trajectories, alternative-token margins, or nonlinear functions of generation-time states.

The swap experiments are suggestive but not definitive: high/low confidence donors are also likely to differ in correctness, question difficulty, answer semantics, and calibration regime. Same-confidence controls reduce generic substitution concerns but do not isolate confidence as the transferred causal variable.

The corrupt-then-restore patching setup mean-ablates answer tokens, causing a severe collapse in behavior. Recovery from this intervention may reflect restoration of answer/content information or generic answer-quality features, not necessarily a cached confidence computation.

Generalization is promising but uneven. The strongest results are for Gemma 3 27B on TriviaQA with a specific prompt. Qwen is smaller, the reasoning model has highly skewed confidence outputs and a null PANL noising result, and some MMLU/BigMath effects are asymmetric or only trends.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed. The appendix gives many procedural details and sample sizes, but the manuscript does not appear to specify a code release, exact splits, judging prompts for GPT-4o-mini correctness labels, or all implementation details needed to reproduce complex hook-based interventions.

The discussion occasionally overreaches toward metacognition, second-order confidence, and introspective awareness. The results support a mechanistic account of a verbal confidence behavior, but those broader cognitive interpretations should be framed more cautiously.

strengths: The paper asks a clear and interesting mechanistic question: when and where LLMs form representations that later support verbal confidence reports.

The empirical program is broad for a mechanistic interpretability paper, combining steering, patching, mean ablation, activation swaps, attention blocking, and probing rather than relying on a single diagnostic.

The use of adjacent control positions, alternative prompt formats, Qwen/Gemma/Magistral checks, and BigMath/MMLU/TriviaQA extensions strengthens the case that the observed PANL/CC effects are not purely accidental.

The manuscript is generally well organized and includes substantial methodological detail in the appendix, including sample sizes, intervention locations, metrics, and an OOD-shift analysis for activation interventions.
The limitations section acknowledges some prompt-sensitivity and routing ambiguities, which is valuable and should not be penalized.
weaknesses: The central claims are overstated. The experiments show that answer-adjacent and confidence-colon activations causally affect prompted confidence tokens, but they do not establish that models perform automatic, sophisticated metacognitive self-evaluation rather than exploiting prompt-, answer-, correctness-, or difficulty-correlated representations.

The paper repeatedly says certain alternatives are “ruled out,” especially just-in-time computation and content-based explanations, but the evidence is weaker. Attention-blocking null results at CC do not exclude information already routed into intermediate tokens or residual states, and the categorical prompt even shows redundant routing that complicates the interpretation.

The patching setup is a fragile basis for causal claims: replacing answer embeddings with mean activations creates a highly artificial corrupted run whose collapse to low confidence may reflect generic disruption. Restoring PANL or CC can recover downstream behavior without proving that PANL stores a dedicated confidence variable.

The activation-swap experiment does not fully separate confidence from correctness, question difficulty, answer semantics, answer length, or dataset artifacts. Same-confidence donor controls help, but they do not guarantee that cross-confidence effects isolate confidence-specific content.

The “not reducible to log-probabilities” conclusion is too strong. The baselines are limited to a small set of linear summaries of answer-token log-probabilities, while activations contain much richer information about the question, answer, dataset, and correctness. This does not prove a second-order confidence computation.

Statistical reporting is underdeveloped. Many figures rely on SEM curves over many layers, positions, scales, datasets, and interventions, but the paper provides little formal hypothesis testing, multiple-comparison handling, effect-size uncertainty, or robustness to random seeds and trial selection.

Generalization remains limited. Most detailed evidence is for Gemma 3 27B on a fixed confidence template; Qwen, Magistral, BigMath, and MMLU are mostly appendix-level replications with some weakened or asymmetric effects, including a non-significant MMLU swap trend and no PANL noising effect for Magistral.

Reproducibility is incomplete for an ICML submission. The paper gives many procedural details but does not appear to provide code, exact seeds, full prompts in machine-readable form, model-loading versions beyond names, or enough information to reproduce GPT-4o-mini answer grading decisions.

The presentation is ambitious but sometimes rhetorically ahead of the evidence, using terms such as “metacognition,” “self-evaluation,” “cached retrieval,” and “ruling out” in places where more cautious language would be more scientifically accurate.

Research ethics and limitations are only lightly treated. The work has direct implications for confidence calibration and possible overtrust in LLM self-reports, but the manuscript does not seriously discuss misuse, deployment risks, or whether mechanistic interventions could make confidence reports more persuasive without being more truthful.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely question: how verbal confidence is internally generated in LLMs, rather than only whether such confidence is calibrated. The cached-retrieval framing is clear, useful, and connects well to both mechanistic interpretability and confidence/metacognition literature.

The empirical case is unusually convergent. Activation steering, patching, noising, swapping, decoding, variance partitioning, and attention blocking all point to PANL and CC as important loci, with earlier effects at PANL and later effects at CC. This substantially strengthens the soundness beyond what a probing-only paper would support.
The causal controls are thoughtful: adjacent-token controls, answer-colon controls, same-confidence activation swaps, OOD-shift checks, and prompt variants help rule out several simple confounds.

The paper makes a meaningful contribution by showing that verbal confidence is not well explained by simple answer-token log-probability summaries; PANL activations explain substantial additional variance. This is a useful empirical result even if one interprets the “second-order” language cautiously.

Generalization experiments add real value: the main pattern is tested across categorical and numeric confidence formats, TriviaQA/BigMath/MMLU, Gemma/Qwen, and a reasoning model with chain-of-thought traces.
The writing is clear and well organized. The roadmap, prompt figures, methodological appendix, and limitations discussion make the paper relatively easy to follow despite many interventions.
weaknesses: Some central claims are phrased more strongly than the evidence fully warrants. The results support cached confidence-relevant representations, but claims such as “automatic sophisticated self-evaluation” and “second-order” confidence are somewhat interpretive; the experiments do not fully distinguish semantic answer-quality evaluation from other hidden correlates beyond the six log-probability summaries.

The “beyond log-probabilities” analysis controls only a small set of scalar answer-token log-probability summaries. It does not rule out more expressive functions of the full token distribution, entropy over plausible answers, retrieval uncertainty, or other generation-time signals available internally.

Attention-blocking null results are not definitive evidence against all just-in-time computation, since information may have flowed earlier or through redundant paths. The paper acknowledges this, but the main-text wording sometimes treats the just-in-time hypothesis as more fully ruled out than the method permits.

Several effects are partial or asymmetric, especially patching/noising and the Magistral/MMLU swap results. The authors give plausible explanations, but these patterns suggest the cached pathway is one contributor among distributed mechanisms rather than a complete mechanistic account.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed in the manuscript. The methods are detailed, but I did not see a code/data release statement, exact trial splits, annotation prompts for GPT-4o-mini correctness grading, or enough implementation detail to make all intervention sweeps straightforward to reproduce.

The experimental scope is still narrow relative to the broad framing: mostly open-weight instruction models, greedy decoding, fixed prompt wording within each format, and relatively controlled QA settings. Sensitivity to paraphrases, adversarial/persona framing, multi-turn contexts, and deployed black-box models remains open.
